sm: The show opens with a clip of Joe Rogan saying Texas went blue in the 2026 cycle because older Republicans pushed marijuana crackdowns reminiscent of reefer madness. Ben Shapiro answers that Rogan, a Los Angeles native, should not bring California values to Texas, pointing to Rogan's votes and endorsements for Gary Johnson, Bernie Sanders and Jo Jorgensen before a last-minute endorsement of Donald Trump in 2024. He says Rogan then turned on Trump over Epstein conspiracy theories and praised Senate-elect James Talarico. Shapiro argues that Trump's 2024 win rested on far more than podcast hosts, including Hispanics and married men and women.

Shapiro says Republicans must decide what they are for, and he names freedom, virtue and strength as the traditional core. His rule is that anyone who cheered or campaigned for Democrats in 2026 should not define the future of the party. He plays Rogan saying podcasters are not press people and that it is a sickness that anyone takes their opinions so seriously, and agrees with him. He applies the same rule to Nick Fuentes, whom he calls a fascist who wants Republicans to keep losing, and to Tucker Carlson, who campaigned against Mike Rogers in Michigan.

Shapiro turns to The Bulwark, saying it pretends to be Republican while celebrating Democratic wins, and plays Sarah Longwell cheering at a conference in Denver. He then walks through an Echelon Insights chart of the electorate. About 31 percent are conservatives, 43 percent are liberals or progressives, 22 percent are socially conservative but economically liberal populists, and only 5 percent are libertarians. He says Democrats need only a minority of the populist box to win, which is why conservatives feel on the edge of panic. Trump moved to the center on economics but not on social issues, and Democrats have now gone quieter on trans issues.

Shapiro says the way forward is to change how people live rather than the electorate itself. In the last cycle married men voted majority Republican, while single men went for Democrats by 57 to 34. He argues that pot, economic nationalism or victimhood will not win young men, because Democrats can offer all of that. In his view the answer is to push them toward upward mobility, marriage and responsibility, which he sums up as be their dad, not their therapist. He adds that the right and the left both now run ecosystems built on victimhood.

Shapiro discusses a Saturday Night Live episode in which John Mulaney and the cast mocked baby boomers in a Woodstock sketch as greedy for owning houses and money. He notes that Mulaney grew up in a wealthy boomer household, and says boomers can be criticized for the entitlement system but that accumulating property is not inherently bad. He is angrier about a bit calling the World War Two generation autistic, which he says mocks men who stormed the beaches of Normandy and then worked factory jobs.

He argues this reflects a culture of victimization toward older generations. Citing a Buckley Institute poll, he notes that 47 percent of students say socialist countries offer a better economic model than American capitalism, while only 33 percent disagree. He says the answer is to offer opportunity along with a kick in the pants, and to tell people that their first duty is to make good decisions in the freest and most prosperous country in history. Otherwise, he warns, you get Texas turning blue because people did not get their weed, and no party worth saving.

Shapiro restates freedom, virtue and strength as the Republican foundation, then says tech at its best embodies all three. He shows video of SpaceX catching a Starship booster with the tower arms nicknamed chopsticks, and reads Walter Isaacson's account of how Elon Musk pushed the idea. He credits free-market competition, noting that a United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed and destroyed 40 Amazon satellites. He also reads Matt Stoller's claim that Musk is not a genius and Musk's reply about Starship, Falcon and Blue Origin.

He then turns to what he calls the Nvidia scandal, tying it to Adam Smith's point that markets need virtue. He lays out a theory in which Chinese money flows through Singapore and Malaysia, including a company tied to Jensen Huang's alleged Chinese-linked mistress, and funds the AI flywheel. He cites Wall Street Journal figures on Nvidia's China revenue and nearly 12 billion dollars of chips sent through Megaspeed. He thinks Huang's exit is really about exposing that chip pipeline, and notes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging new leadership and a clash with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnik.

Shapiro cites the New York Times on a Malaysian data center whose operator is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnik once led, and warns of family members of officials profiting. He says Lutnik may be in trouble, and plays All-In hosts saying Nvidia effectively acted as the bank for the AI economy through Huang. He reads Wall Street Journal reporting that Nvidia is pulling back its open checkbook for AI startups. He closes with reports that Huang may seek a comeback and that investor Brad Gerstner is urging the board to leave that option open.

Shapiro says some Republicans still articulate an inspiring conservatism, chiefly Secretary of State Marco Rubio. He plays Rubio at the Federalist Society saying Americans are bound not by ethnicity but as descendants of go-getters who refused limits, and that living in America differs from becoming an American. He plays Rubio defending engagement abroad for national security, markets and stability in the hemisphere. He plays Rubio denouncing international law as an instrument of a global elite, and warning that the spirit of Marx lives on in efforts to abolish the distinctions between nations.

Turning to Democrats, Shapiro says Maryland Governor Wes Moore is slipping in prediction markets after a New York Post report. The report says Moore wrote that he wept at his grandfather's funeral over the death of a comrade who was in fact still alive at the time. Shapiro adds that Moore has also lied about a Bronze Star. He then plays Senator Chris Van Hollen announcing a run for Senate majority leader, and Hasan Piker saying old white men are needed to sell the party's message.

Shapiro covers New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's order to disband the NYPD Strategic Response Group, which polices protests and handles counterterrorism. A civilian Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division will take over protests, though not until 2028, with a First Amendment Support Team in the interim. Tear gas, pepper spray, loud acoustic devices, bicycles and kettling would be banned. Shapiro plays Mamdani being asked who would respond to terrorist threats and saying the two roles are not the same. Shapiro says this unleashes the mob.

Shapiro interviews investigative journalist Andy Ngo about his new book on the Zizians, which he describes as a trans death cult. Ngo says it is one of the deadliest cults in recent American history, and that his research began with an ambush shooting of a Border Patrol agent in Vermont. He found that the linked suspects were all trans-identifying and part of a cult led by a figure using the alias Ziz. He says the group is tied to at least eight deaths, and that members have avoided convictions by filing frivolous accusations and lawsuits claiming transphobic persecution.

Shapiro says some ideologies create permission structures for violence, noting that trans radicals call denial of gender identity genocide. Ngo describes a 2022 sword and knife attack on elderly landlord Curtis Lind, in which one attacker was killed. He says activists raised money for that attacker as a victim, and that Senate Democrats later read the name aloud in a resolution. Ngo links growing trans violence to radicalizing ideology, firearms, mental health conditions and hormone use, says the Justice Department is only now soliciting research, and says it will take multiple administrations.
